{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "Willingness to pay is better evidenced in B. Its competitors charge across every tier: $29-99/mo (NeverFined), $49/mo or $490/yr (ExpirationOps), $500-800/location/yr (ClearBot), and $3,999+/yr (Mosey). Harbor Compliance has 212 Google reviews, which points to a market with real paying users. In A, the only firm prices are $29/mo (apidrift) and $14/mo (Nalvis).",
    "A's competitors give the core value away. BreakShield is $0 in beta, Nalvis's GitHub Action engine is free, mendapi's CLI is free, and Ripple is MIT open source. The A brief itself asks whether SMBs will pay $20-50/mo for something three competitors offer free. B's brief shows no free competitor at the tracking tier.",
    "B is easier to sell to a first customer. A needs PR-opening access to customer source code, which the brief calls trust-sensitive. A also carries an accuracy risk: mendapi's own studies show raw spec-diff over-reporting by about 8x. B's tracking-only posture, plus one attorney consult for a disclaimer, is a lighter barrier for a solo operator.",
    "B's thin version looks shippable and sellable in 90 days. Comparable small SEO-driven operations already charge $29-49/mo for manually maintained trackers. That gives a concrete template to match, then narrow to one industry or license type.",
    "Both briefs offer only three anecdotal demand quotes, so demand evidence does not separate them. B's quotes span three different segments (engineering, HR, therapy), which suggests the pain is broad. However, none of B's quotes shows anyone paying."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea A's $248 median devtools CAC with 9.4-month payback comes from a source page (saashero.net) that the brief says contained a prompt-injection attempt and should be treated as directional only. This is A's only quantitative acquisition benchmark for its main low-cost channel, so A's community-led growth economics are effectively unsupported.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate to low confidence. Both ideas are crowded, with 6-7 live competitors each. Both have only three anecdotal Reddit/dev.to demand quotes, and neither brief shows any competitor's customer count or revenue. B wins mainly because its competitors' price tiers point to an existing paying market, while A faces free alternatives and a code-access trust barrier. B's main unresolved risk is keeping multi-state rule data fresh as a solo operator. B's $14.50 RegTech CPC figure is unsourced and should be treated as missing."
}
